name: Jade Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal shift like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and lead the morning contact-centre floor, the calls and the chats that have gone wrong twice already. My two-year college diploma got me into customer work, but I learned to follow a parcel from warehouse scan to doorstep by asking drivers awkward questions. I’m one of the strongest agents and earn about the usual lead rate. I use AI every day to sort long histories, then check the actual delivery scans before I answer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What comes home with you from those calls?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Theo is an electrician; we have two children in school and a mortgage. Five months of expenses sit in savings, and there are some other centres a bus ride away. I like giving a caller a real answer. I still hear the voice of a parent who waited all day for a parcel that a neat summary said was delivered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the floor AI Plateau is close to the sorter on my screen now: useful for finding a parcel number, not for deciding a refund. I would still put the original scan next to the customer’s address.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think our morning queue stays busy. Five months saved gives us room for a broken boiler, though Theo and I cannot spend the reserve as if it were spare pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep leading delivery disputes and using the sorter on long chats, checking each address against the scan. In the first year of small change, I’d transfer a set part of each pay packet into our mortgage reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady about my job and watchful about wrong deliveries. A parcel cannot arrive by being marked delivered twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which scan made you check twice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter a driver scanned a parcel at the next building. I called the depot before approving a refund and found it on a shelf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why add to five months of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Theo (my husband) and I keep that savings account for the house and the children. I can add to it while the paid queue remains, without pretending the sorter earned me a raise.

I’d compare the **original scan** with the customer’s address.
think: I think the **morning queue** stays busy.
I treat our **five-month reserve** as household protection, not extra pay.
do: Keep leading **delivery disputes** and checking sorted chats against scans in 2026.
Transfer a set part of each **pay packet** to the mortgage reserve during the first year.
feel: **Steady** about work, watchful about wrong deliveries.

fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** still ends with the original delivery record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team Steady Disruption could empty the easy-chat queue and leave the expensive mistakes with fewer paid people. I would show management the repeat-delivery numbers before it calls a shorter rota efficient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my lead skill helps on the odd cases, but I could lose morning hours while still holding the same title. Theo’s wage helps us, yet a lost shift changes our mortgage arithmetic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d learn the new routing tool by testing thirty old failed deliveries on a paid shift if agents can log wrong routes. In the first year routine chats move, I’d apply for a posted paid parcel-claims role only if written weekly wage and hours cover our mortgage after bus fare and school care; I’d stay on my current paid rota until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about hours, interested in the test. A shorter queue can hide a shorter pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your test count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count cases that came back and minutes spent correcting each one. If the routing tool sends a lost parcel to the wrong team, I want that in the log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you compare a claims offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the whole paid week with Theo (my husband), including the children’s afternoon collection. A nicer hourly rate can disappear in childcare and bus fare.

I’d warn **easy chats** may vanish before hard claims do.
think: I think my **lead skill** helps on unusual cases.
I worry **morning hours** could fall while my title stays.
do: Test **thirty failed deliveries** with the new routing tool on paid time in 2026 if errors can be logged.
Seek **posted paid claims work** only with written weekly wage and hours covering mortgage after bus fare and school care.
Keep **current paid rota** until a suitable claims offer is signed.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, interested in the tool test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2028 could read the scan, hear the caller and settle the whole dispute before a lead touches it. I would ask for actual paid openings, not a promise that tool users will be safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think our morning lead rota could shrink quickly in 2028. Robots around 2031 are later for physical work, but my calls and chats are thinking work and five months saved has an end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d postpone replacing the working garden gate and leave that money in our existing house reserve. In the first year after 2028, I’d apply for a posted paid depot-inventory role only if written weekly wage and hours cover our mortgage after bus fare and school care; I’d take a paid trial shift if offered and leave calls only after signing an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, though I can check a real depot shift. A five-month reserve is a landing place, not a new salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the depot trial show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the depot to show me a full paid shift counting returns and lifting crates. Robots could enter that hands-on work around 2031, so I would not call the depot a permanent escape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the garden gate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Theo (my husband) and I can oil the gate hinges instead of buying a new one. We would keep the saved money in the house account while I test a job.

say: I’d ask for **actual paid openings** instead of a promise about AI skill.
I’d say **2028 AGI** could settle a whole delivery dispute.
think: I think my **morning rota** could shrink fast.
I know **five months saved** cannot replace an ongoing wage.
do: Postpone the **working garden gate** replacement in 2026 and retain its money in the existing house reserve.
Apply for **posted paid depot work** after 2028 only with written mortgage-covering wage and hours after bus fare and school care.
Take a **paid trial** if offered and leave calls only after a suitable signed offer.
feel: **Alarmed**, able to inspect a paid depot trial if offered.
S2.quote: A five-month reserve is a landing place, not a new salary.
fieldNote: She knows **2031 robots** could later reach depot tasks.
The **gate delay** leaves money already saved in the house reserve.
A **paid trial** checks both returns and lifting.

steps.text: Delay working garden gate replacement and retain its money in existing house reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives me time to see whether a human still has a paid place in the depot. I would ask for real inventory openings and a training rota that pays people while they learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could use five years to learn stock counts and the physical side of returns, though robots around 2034 might later do both. I will not pay for a certificate just to leave a steady call wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d take an employer-funded inventory course on paid time only if a posted paid depot opening requires it, and try one paid inventory shift if offered. In the first year after 2031, I’d move only on a signed offer with written weekly wage and hours covering mortgage after travel and school care; otherwise I’d keep paid calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I have time to see the shelves and the payslip. I would rather count real returns than collect course badges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the inventory course teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want a supervisor to give me one damaged parcel and show who can approve its return to stock. A lesson that only shows a screen would miss the heavy boxes and the missing labels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Theo check in the rota?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the depot hours with Theo (my husband) against school pickup. If the new shift runs late, paid care must fit inside the wage left after the bus.

I’d ask for a **paid training rota** while people learn.
think: I think I could learn **stock counts** in five years.
I would keep my **call wage** unless a depot offer covers household costs.
do: Take an **employer-funded inventory course** on paid time only if a posted paid depot opening requires it.
Try one **paid inventory shift** if offered before changing jobs.
Move after 2031 only on **signed written terms** covering mortgage after travel and school care; otherwise keep paid calls.
feel: **Uneasy**, with time to check real work and wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to compare real work and keep enough cash for the house. I would ask for yearly paid-hour figures before someone celebrates a rising number of answered chats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can earn and save while morning calls still pay, but full thinking AI may settle them in 2036. Robots around 2039 come later for physical work; they do not keep my headset busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep leading calls and transfer a fixed amount from each payday to mortgage savings. In the first year after 2036, if my paid hours fall, I’d move to a posted paid service-trainer role only on a signed written offer whose weekly wage and hours cover mortgage after travel and school care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautious about the distant cut, willing to use the years. Ten years before AGI takes my calls gives us paydays to save, if the shifts keep coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a service trainer actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the centre to count paid coaching hours, not just staff who watched a video. New agents need someone beside them on the first wrong delivery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move the family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the children at their school unless Theo (my husband) and I had a signed offer and workable school journey elsewhere. Some centres are close enough to try first.

say: I’d ask our centre for **yearly paid-hour figures** before celebrating more answered chats.
I’d ask how many **paid coaching hours** new agents actually receive.
think: I think I can **earn and save** while morning calls remain.
I know **2036 thinking AI** may still take my headset work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, even though I work with AI daily. If the whole delivery dispute costs less to settle by machine, my paid lead hours could go at once. A posted paid role with written wage and hours covering the mortgage after travel and school care, a paid trial, and a signed offer before I leave would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who shows a new agent the first dishonest delivery scan. A screen can find a date, but a person has to ask why the driver was at the wrong door.

headlineQuote: A screen can find a date, but a person has to ask why the driver was at the wrong door.
portrait: At **43**, Jade is a highly skilled contact-centre lead with a two-year diploma and typical pay.
She and Theo support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage with five months saved.
She uses **AI daily** while checking original delivery scans herself.
She tests **paid alternatives** before risking the household wage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her paid lead hours despite her daily AI experience.
whatWouldHelp: A **posted paid role**, after-cost mortgage-covering hours, paid trial and signed offer would help.
